questions.q: What does 'disagree and commit' actually mean, according to the lesson?
options: Genuinely supporting a decision's execution after your case wasn't accepted, not quietly going through the motions while resenting the outcome
Pretending to agree with a decision while secretly undermining it
Refusing to ever voice disagreement with any decision
Always reversing your position to match whatever the majority decided
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly distinguishes real commitment from passive resistance disguised as commitment -- the second isn't actually disagree-and-commit at all, even if it looks similar on the surface.

questions.q: Why does re-litigating a lost architecture argument in a smaller side conversation damage a team's decision-making ability, beyond just failing to change the outcome?
options: It introduces the risk that every future decision could be reopened through a side channel instead of staying settled once made, which makes teams move slower on all decisions, not just the contested one
Side conversations are always technically more productive than the original decision meeting
Re-litigating has no real effect on anything beyond the single decision being discussed
This behavior is always rewarded and encouraged in healthy engineering teams
questions.explain: The damage isn't limited to one decision -- once a team learns decisions can be reopened through side channels, trust in ALL settled decisions erodes, slowing the team down broadly.

questions.q: What is the healthy way to register real disagreement during a decision-making process, per the lesson?
options: Make the case clearly and specifically during the actual decision conversation, ideally in writing (an ADR's or design doc's Alternatives Considered), then voice continued disagreement once through the right channel before committing
Stay completely silent during the decision, then raise objections afterward in private
Never voice disagreement under any circumstances, even during the decision conversation itself
Repeatedly raise the same objection in every subsequent meeting indefinitely
questions.explain: Disagree-and-commit doesn't mean staying silent -- it means making the case clearly where the decision is actually being made, then committing once the decision is final, rather than reopening it repeatedly.

questions.q: According to the lesson, when is disagree-and-commit the WRONG approach, and escalation the right one instead?
options: When the disagreement involves serious, hard-to-reverse consequences (a security vulnerability, a legal/compliance violation, an extremely costly-to-undo choice)
Disagree-and-commit is always correct in every situation with no exceptions
Escalation is only appropriate for disagreements about coding style
Escalation should be used for every disagreement, regardless of stakes
questions.explain: The test given is whether a wrong decision's cost would be absorbable and a learning opportunity (disagree-and-commit fits) or genuinely difficult to undo (escalation is the right call instead).

questions.q: What is the test the lesson gives for deciding between disagree-and-commit and escalation?
options: Whether committing to the decision, if it turns out wrong, would cause a cost the team can absorb and learn from, or a cost that's genuinely difficult to undo
Whether the disagreement involves more than two people
Whether the original decision was made in a large meeting or a small one
Whether the disagreeing engineer has more seniority than the decision-maker
questions.explain: The lesson's explicit test is about the reversibility and severity of being wrong -- an absorbable, learnable cost favors disagree-and-commit; a hard-to-reverse, serious cost favors escalating instead.
